introduction-the-physics-of-decision-mak.core: Tools change every few years, but the way you decide does not. Engineering judgement, meaning good decisions under uncertainty, is a learnable skill built on thinking frameworks.

first_principles.problem: Engineers learn Kubernetes, Terraform and AWS, then the landscape shifts (Mesos, Swarm, bare metal all had their turn). Teams that only know tools keep re-learning, and they make expensive architecture choices by copying whatever is popular.
truths: Tool knowledge decays quickly.
Architecture decisions outlive the tools they were made with.
Decision quality can be improved with deliberate method.
derivation: Treat **your thinking** as the most critical component to debug.
Learn the two basic modes: **copying what works (analogy)** and **deriving from facts (first principles)**.
Choose deliberately between them, which is what **engineering judgement** means.

analogy.title: A pilot vs. an autopilot user
analogy.story: Someone who only knows the autopilot buttons is stuck when the autopilot fails or a new aircraft arrives. A pilot who understands lift and drag can fly anything, because they know *why* the buttons do what they do.
analogy.breaks: Aircraft physics never changes. Engineering constraints (team, budget, scale) do, so the facts must be re-checked for each decision.

example.title: Picking an orchestrator in 2015 vs 2026
example.scenario: A team chose Mesos in 2015 because "Twitter uses it".

steps.label: Analogy
steps.detail: "Twitter uses Mesos" told them nothing about their own needs.

steps.label: Judgement
steps.detail: "We need to run 40 stateless services with 3 engineers" points to a managed, simple option.

example.outcome: decisions are anchored in your facts, so they survive tool churn.

points: Two modes: analogy and first principles.

check.q: Why is engineering judgement more durable than tool knowledge?
check.a: It's based on constraints and reasoning that apply to any tool, while specific tools get replaced every few years.

what-is-reasoning-by-analogy.core: Reasoning by analogy means copying the solution of a similar problem someone already solved. It's fast and lowers risk, but it silently assumes their context matches yours.

first_principles.problem: "Netflix uses microservices, so we should too." The logic hides an assumption: that your scale, team and constraints are similar enough for their answer to fit. When they aren't, you inherit their costs without their benefits.
truths: Humans are pattern-matching machines by default.
Proven solutions have known failure modes.
Two situations can look alike but differ in what matters.
derivation: Use analogy for **speed**: you don't re-derive a CI pipeline every time.
Use it for **lower risk**: proven, documented, with community support.
Always ask the hidden question: **is their context really like mine?**

analogy.title: Borrowing a recipe
analogy.story: You copy a friend's lasagne recipe. That works perfectly if you have the same oven, ingredients and number of guests. For 50 guests with half the oven size, the same recipe fails.
analogy.breaks: Recipes come with quantities you can see. Architectures rarely say which constraints they depended on.

example.title: "Stack Overflow says add Redis"
example.scenario: A team with 200 requests/minute adds a Redis caching layer because a blog post did.

steps.label: Analogy
steps.detail: The blog's site had 50,000 requests/s and a slow database.

steps.label: Check
steps.detail: This team's database answered in 2 ms, so the cache solved nothing.

example.outcome: you learn to ask whether the reference case actually matches before copying.

points: Fast and low-risk when contexts match.

check.q: What hidden assumption does every analogy make?
check.a: That your situation is similar enough, in the ways that matter, for the other solution to work.

what-is-first-principles-reasoning.core: First-principles reasoning breaks a problem down to facts that are true regardless of convention (physics, maths, budget, team size) and builds the solution up from those.

first_principles.problem: When nothing off the shelf fits, or the stakes are high, copying is risky. You need a way to find the right answer for your situation, which means reasoning from what you know to be true, not from what others did.
truths: Physics sets hard limits (~70 ms Virginia–Frankfurt round trip).
Maths sets capacity (1,000 req/s × 50 ms = 50 concurrent workers).
Budget and team size are real constraints too.
derivation: **Question** every assumption: is this true, or just common?
**Decompose** to the bedrock facts of your situation.
**Rebuild** a solution that satisfies those facts, and only those.

analogy.title: Building with Lego from the box of bricks
analogy.story: Instead of buying the pre-designed kit, you look at the bricks you actually have and the shape you actually need, then design a model that fits both.
analogy.breaks: Lego bricks are visible. Engineering constraints often hide in assumptions nobody wrote down, so finding them is most of the work.

example.title: Sizing a worker pool
example.scenario: 1,000 requests/s, each taking 50 ms. How many workers?

steps.label: Facts
steps.detail: Arrival rate and service time are measured, not assumed.

steps.label: Derive
steps.detail: Concurrency = rate × time = 50, so anything less queues.

steps.label: Build
steps.detail: Provision about 70 for headroom, regardless of what any blog recommends.

example.outcome: a number derived from your facts instead of copied from someone else's setup.

check.q: Give an example of a first principle in engineering.
check.a: The speed of light sets a minimum latency between regions; a fixed budget or team size limits what you can run.

the-chef-vs-the-cook.core: The cook follows recipes without knowing why each step exists. The chef understands what each ingredient does, so can adapt when context changes or something is missing.

first_principles.problem: Following recipes works until conditions change: high altitude, a missing ingredient, a new kind of dish. Engineers who only copy patterns ("Facebook uses React") are stuck when their context differs from the recipe's.
truths: Every step in a recipe serves a function.
Knowing the function lets you substitute.
Contexts change constantly.
derivation: For each practice, ask **what function it serves** (sugar: sweetness, browning, moisture, structure).
When context changes, **keep the function, change the form**.
Use recipes for routine work, but understand them for anything that matters.

analogy.title: Out of sugar
analogy.story: The cook without sugar is stuck. The chef knows sugar provides sweetness, browning and moisture, so they pick honey or reduce the quantity based on which function the dish needs.
analogy.breaks: Cooking chemistry is well documented. In engineering the 'function' of a practice is often undocumented, so you have to dig for it.

example.title: Kubernetes without the why
example.scenario: A 3-person team adopts Kubernetes because 'it's what serious companies use'.

steps.label: Function
steps.detail: They need easy deploys, health restarts and scaling.

steps.label: Substitute
steps.detail: A managed platform provides those without running a cluster.

example.outcome: the team keeps the function and drops the cost that came with the copied form.

points: Keep the function, change the form.
Be a chef where it matters.

check.q: What does a chef do that a cook can't?
check.a: Substitute or invent, because they know the function each ingredient or step serves.

cargo-cult-engineering.core: Cargo cult engineering copies the visible form of a successful practice while missing the invisible function that made it work, then waits for results that never come.

first_principles.problem: After WWII, islanders built bamboo control towers and coconut headphones, waiting for planes. They copied what success looked like, not what caused it. Teams do the same with "Spotify squads", microservices or daily standups.
truths: The form of a practice is easy to see and copy.
The function behind it is often invisible.
Results come from function, not form.
derivation: For each practice you copy, list its **form** (what it looks like).
Then list its **function** (the mechanism that produces results).
If you can't name the function, you're likely cargo-culting.
Adopt only practices whose function you need and can reproduce.

analogy.title: Bamboo control towers
analogy.story: The islanders' runway looked right and the rituals were performed correctly, but there was no radio, no fuel and no logistics network. The planes don't land.
analogy.breaks: Islanders eventually saw no planes. Software teams often don't notice, because the copied practice looks busy and productive.

example.title: Copying "Spotify squads"
example.scenario: A 30-person company renames teams to squads, tribes and guilds.

steps.label: Form
steps.detail: New names, new org chart.

steps.label: Missing function
steps.detail: Years of trust, autonomy, tooling and alignment practices.

steps.label: Better
steps.detail: Identify the actual coordination problem and fix that.

example.outcome: you stop copying appearances and start copying mechanisms.

points: Form is visible, function is hidden.

check.q: How do you tell if a practice is cargo cult?
check.a: If the team can't explain the mechanism by which it produces results in their context.

the-first-principles-algorithm.core: First principles as a repeatable method: identify assumptions, break the problem into fundamental truths, rebuild a solution from those, then validate it.

first_principles.problem: "Think from first principles" sounds abstract. Without a method, people either skip it or never finish. Langley scaled up steam models (analogy) and crashed. The Wright brothers asked what flight requires, found control was the unsolved part, and flew for under $1,000.
truths: Hidden assumptions drive most decisions.
Complex problems decompose into independent subproblems.
A design must be tested against reality.
derivation: **1. Identify assumptions**: write down what everyone 'knows'.
**2. Break down** to fundamental truths (physics, maths, constraints).
**3. Rebuild** from those truths only.
**4. Validate** with measurement or a small experiment.

analogy.title: The Wright brothers' wind tunnel
analogy.story: Everyone assumed more engine power was the answer. The Wrights decomposed flight into lift, thrust and control, saw that control was the real gap, tested 200 wing shapes, and only then added an engine.
analogy.breaks: Flight physics is stable. Your system's constraints shift as usage grows, so the algorithm must be re-run, not done once.

example.title: "We need a bigger database"
example.scenario: Latency is high, and the team assumes the database is too small.

steps.label: Assumption
steps.detail: "Bigger database" was never measured.

steps.label: Truth
steps.detail: Tracing shows the time is in a query loop, not database capacity.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: A code fix beats a costly upgrade.

example.outcome: the real bottleneck is fixed, cheaply, and with evidence.

check.q: What did the Wright brothers do differently from Langley?
check.a: They decomposed flight into subproblems, found control was unsolved, and tested systematically instead of scaling up existing designs.

when-to-use-each-mode.core: First principles is powerful but expensive, and analogy is cheap but context-dependent. Use analogy for common, low-stakes, reversible decisions, and first principles for novel, high-stakes, irreversible ones.

first_principles.problem: Deriving everything from scratch means you never ship. Copying everything means you inherit mismatched decisions. The skill is choosing the right mode for each decision.
truths: Time and attention are limited.
Some decisions are cheap to reverse and some aren't.
Reference cases match some contexts and not others.
derivation: **Analogy** when: the problem is common, stakes are low, context matches, it's quick to validate, it's reversible (Type 2).
**First principles** when: nothing fits, stakes are high, context differs, it's hard to reverse (Type 1).
Often combine them: derive the requirements, then pick a proven tool that meets them.

analogy.title: Choosing a route
analogy.story: For your daily commute you follow the usual road. For moving house across the country, you plan the route from scratch based on your truck, timing and budget.
analogy.breaks: A commute's cost is obvious. In engineering, irreversibility often isn't, so decide that first.

example.title: Lint config vs. database choice

steps.label: Lint
steps.detail: Cheap, reversible, so use the team's standard and move on.

steps.label: Database
steps.detail: Expensive to change, so derive needs (consistency, scale, team skills) first.

example.outcome: effort goes where the consequences are.

points: Match the mode to the stakes.
Derive needs, then reuse proven tools.

check.q: Why not use first principles for every decision?
check.a: It's slow and costly. For routine, reversible choices a proven pattern is the better use of time.

common-pitfalls-and-misconceptions.core: First principles tells you what properties you need, not that you should build everything yourself. Analogy used deliberately isn't laziness, and every 'best practice' is only best for a specific context.

first_principles.problem: People misuse both modes: "first principles" becomes an excuse for Not-Invented-Here rebuilds, "best practice" becomes a reason not to think, and careful analogy gets dismissed as laziness.
truths: Existing tools often already provide the properties you need.
Context determines whether a practice is good.
Time spent re-deriving known answers is waste.
derivation: **Derive properties** you need from first principles.
**Evaluate existing solutions** against those properties (informed analogy).
**Build custom** only when nothing meets your specific constraints.
Mentally append '…for companies like X' to every 'best practice'.

analogy.title: Designing a car vs. buying tyres
analogy.story: Knowing exactly what grip and size you need is first-principles thinking. It doesn't mean you should invent and manufacture your own tyres.
analogy.breaks: Tyre specs are standardised. Software properties are fuzzier, so write them down explicitly before comparing tools.

example.title: "Let's build our own key-value store"
example.scenario: A team derives that it needs a fast, replicated key-value store.

steps.label: Properties
steps.detail: Sub-ms reads, replication, 10 GB of data.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.detail: An existing store satisfies all of them.

steps.label: Decision
steps.detail: Building one would cost months for no benefit.

example.outcome: first-principles clarity leads to the right off-the-shelf choice, not a vanity rebuild.

points: Best practice = best for a context.

check.q: What's the correct order of steps?
check.a: Derive the properties you need, evaluate existing solutions against them, and build custom only if none fits.
